back: The Earth spinning on its axis, once about every 24 hours.

front: How long does the Earth take to orbit the Sun?
back: About 365¼ days (one year). The extra quarter day is why we have a leap year every four years.
The tilt of Earth's axis (about 23.5°). The hemisphere tilted towards the Sun gets higher, more concentrated sunlight and longer days, so it has summer.

front: When are NZ's longest and shortest days?
back: Longest: around 21–22 December. Shortest: around 21 June.

front: Why does the Moon have phases?
back: Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun. As it orbits the Earth, we see different amounts of the lit half.

front: How long is one cycle of Moon phases?
back: About 29.5 days (new moon to new moon).
Waxing: the lit part is growing (after new moon). Waning: the lit part is shrinking (after full moon).
The Moon passes between the Sun and the Earth, and its shadow falls on Earth. It can only happen at new moon.
The Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon, and Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. It can only happen at full moon.
The Māori name for the star cluster also called the Pleiades. Its rising before dawn in midwinter marks the Māori New Year for many iwi.
The star Rigel. Some iwi, for example in Taranaki and Whanganui, use its rising to mark the new year.

front: What three things is Matariki a time for?
back: Remembering those who have died, celebrating the present (gathering and sharing food), and planning for the year ahead.
The Māori lunar calendar. Each night of the Moon's cycle has a name, and it guides activities such as planting, harvesting and fishing. It differs between iwi.
Using where stars rise and set on the horizon, plus ocean swells, winds, birds and clouds.

front: The planets in order from the Sun
back: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune (My Very Eager Mother Just Served Us Nachos).
Inner (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars): small and rocky. Outer (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune): giants made mostly of gas and ice.
The average distance from the Earth to the Sun, about 150 million km.
The distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 trillion km. It is a distance, not a time.

front: How long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
back: About 8 minutes (light travels at about 300,000 km/s).

front: Why is Venus hotter than Mercury?
back: Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat in a very strong greenhouse effect (over 450 °C).

front: Which side of a waxing Moon is lit, seen from NZ?
back: The left side. In the Northern Hemisphere it's the right side.

front: What is a **dwarf planet**? Give an example.
back: A round body that orbits the Sun but hasn't cleared other objects from its orbit, e.g. Pluto (reclassified in 2006).
